```{r}
umd_courses <- read_csv("data/courses.csv")
```
Set-Up: Creating Courses Fall-Spring semesters only 

```{r}
#finding total of courses taught by each professor in the fall and spring terms from 2017 to 2023
courses_fall_spring <- umd_courses |>
  mutate(
    year = as.integer(substr(term, 1, 4)),
    sem_code = substr(term, 5, 6)
  ) %>%
  filter(
    year >= 2017, year <= 2025,
    sem_code %in% c("01", "08")
  ) %>%
  select(-year, -sem_code) 

#creating a column for standard semester dates 
courses_fall_spring <- courses_fall_spring |>
  mutate(
    term_code = as.character(term),
    year = str_sub(term_code, 1, 4),
    term_suffix = str_sub(term_code, 5, 6),
    start_date = case_when(
      term_suffix == "01" ~ ymd(paste0(year, "-01-24")),  
      term_suffix == "08" ~ ymd(paste0(year, "-08-26")),  
      TRUE ~ NA_Date_
    )) |>
  select(-term_code, -term_suffix, -year)

view(courses_fall_spring)

```


Q1: Popular discourse often claims that humanities are declining while STEM fields dominate the future. To explore this at a micro level, calculate the total seat percentages for the English and Computer Science departments during fall semesters. Do you observe any patterns or notable differences? If so, provide an analysis explaining why these differences might exist.

The English department offered 52,394 seats total in the fall from 2018 to 2023. Fall 2023 had the lowest total seats (n= 7,678) and lowest percentage of total (14.65%), approximately 2.3 percentage points lower than most other years. This is a noticeable contraction or decreased of total seats. From 2018 through 2022, seat totals range from 8,700 to 9,200, percentages cluster tightly around ~17%, even Fall 2020, with the pandemic as an independent variable, stays within this band. This change suggests there was a consistent variable in the previous years that is now absent or much lower thus impacting the total number of seats in Fall 2023; It could be university policies, enrollment trends, economic pressures (job market) or instructor availability. 


```{r}
fall_english_department <- courses_fall_spring |>
filter(department == "English", 
        month(start_date) == 8) |>
  mutate(year = year(start_date))


fall_CS_department <- courses_fall_spring |>
filter(department == "Computer Science", 
        month(start_date) == 8) |>
  mutate(year = year(start_date))


fall_journalism_department <- courses_fall_spring |>
filter(department == "Journalism", 
        month(start_date) == 8) |>
  mutate(year = year(start_date))

fall_elec_and_comp_engineering_department <- courses_fall_spring |>
filter(department == "Electrical & Computer Engineering", 
        month(start_date) == 8) |>
  mutate(year = year(start_date))

# Some courses are exactly the same but have special lettering for honors students so this standardizes the id column so we get clean percentages 

fall_english_department <- fall_english_department |>
   mutate(base_course = str_extract(id, "^[A-Z]+\\d+"))|>
  select(-id) |>
  rename(id= base_course)

fall_CS_department <- fall_CS_department |>
   mutate(base_course = str_extract(id, "^[A-Z]+\\d+"))|>
  select(-id) |>
  rename(id= base_course)


fall_journalism_department <- fall_journalism_department |>
   mutate(base_course = str_extract(id, "^[A-Z]+\\d+"))|>
  select(-id) |>
  rename(id= base_course)

fall_elec_and_comp_engineering_department <- fall_elec_and_comp_engineering_department |> 
   mutate(base_course = str_extract(id, "^[A-Z]+\\d+"))|>
  select(-id) |>
  rename(id= base_course)

view(fall_english_department)
view(fall_journalism_department)
view(fall_journalism_department)
view(fall_elec_and_comp_engineering_department)
```


Creating data frames with total percentages seat for each department we're interested in observing
```{r}
#English 
seats_by_year_english <- fall_english_department |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(
    total_seats = sum(seats, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

seats_by_year_english <- seats_by_year_english |>
  mutate(
    percent_of_total = total_seats / sum(total_seats) * 100
  )

#Computer Science 
seats_by_year_CS <- fall_CS_department |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(
    total_seats = sum(seats, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

seats_by_year_CS <- seats_by_year_CS |>
  mutate(
    percent_of_total = total_seats / sum(total_seats) * 100
  )

#Journalism
seats_by_year_journalism <- fall_journalism_department |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(
    total_seats = sum(seats, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

seats_by_year_journalism <- seats_by_year_journalism |>
  mutate(
    percent_of_total = total_seats / sum(total_seats) * 100
  )

#Business and Management 
seats_by_year_elec_and_comp_engineering<- fall_elec_and_comp_engineering_department |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(
    total_seats = sum(seats, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

seats_by_year_elec_and_comp_engineering <- seats_by_year_elec_and_comp_engineering |>
  mutate(
    percent_of_total = total_seats / sum(total_seats) * 100
  )

view(seats_by_year_english)
view(seats_by_year_CS)
view(seats_by_year_journalism)
view(seats_by_year_elec_and_comp_engineering)
```


Q2: Which departments had the least amount of professors across the years? which ones had the most? Are there any patterns in the results? 

A2: The departments Business and Management and English had the most amount of professors for the spring and fall semesters between 2018 to 2023. Though Business and Management also had the highest number of seats across the observed semesters, the English department wider ratio of more professors than total seats per observed semester. This is probably because a lot of english courses are seminars or independent studies

Q3: [wildcard] Search the description column for keywords of interest and discuss findings (if a pattern is found, if not keep searching relevant words) 

A3: We were curious to see what courses, in which semesters, had the word Trump in their description. We found 10, all of them relevant to the president. Out of the 10 courses mentioning Trump in the data (checked with the out of session semesters), six are journalism courses. We found this out by searching Trump in courses_fall_spring's description column. Five courses were offered in spring 2021, four from the journalism department and one from Government and Politics. The classes started some weeks after the Jan. 6 insurrection at the U.S. capitol. This isn't a newsworthy finding but it does reflect well on the Journalism school that the knee jerk reaction was to teach students how to navigate increased bias in reporting and stay afloat in the fierce battle to control the flow of information. So, we see these courses, the moment they began and their focus on Trump as a reflection of Philip Merrill's focus on teaching its students real-world journalism.

```{r}
trump_courses <- courses_fall_spring |>
  mutate( title = str_to_upper(title), description = str_to_upper(description)) |>
  filter(str_detect(description, "TRUMP"))|>
  group_by(start_date) |>
summarise(
  semester_total = n(),
  .groups = "drop"
) |>
arrange(desc(start_date))


trump_courses |>
  ggplot() + 
  geom_line(aes(x=start_date, y=semester_total), size=1.2)+

labs(title = "Mentions of Trump in Course Description", x= "Semester", y = "Number of Mentions")+
  scale_y_continuous(n.breaks = 15) +
    scale_x_date(
    breaks = artificial_intelligence$start_date,
    date_labels = "%b %Y"  
  ) +
  theme_minimal()+
   theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 25,  hjust=1),
     plot.margin = margin(10, 10, 35, 10)
  )

```


Q4: Is there a change in the mentions of Artificial intelligence in courses?

A4: Through this question we hoped to find out whether the recent uptick in AI usage throughout the world is reflected in the course offerings at UMD. While this data set is two years old there is still a significant increase in the number of courses with a focus on AI. The biggest increase was from the Fall 2022 semester to the Spring 2023 semester where the number of courses more than doubled. This is likely due to the release of ChatGPT in November of 2022. Even though the number of courses dropped again in Fall 2023, it shows how there was a continued interest in AI throughout UMD. 

```{r}

artificial_intelligence <- courses_fall_spring |>
  mutate( title = str_to_upper(title), description = str_to_upper(description)) |>
  
  filter(
    str_detect(title,"ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE") | str_detect(description, "ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE") | str_detect(title, " AI ") | str_detect(description, " AI ")) |>
  group_by(start_date) |>
summarise(
  semester_total = n(),
  .groups = "drop"
) |>
arrange(desc(start_date))
 
artificial_intelligence |>
  ggplot() + 
  geom_line(aes(x=start_date, y=semester_total), size=1.2)+

labs(title = "Mentions of Artificial Intelligence in Course Title and Description", x= "Semester", y = "Number of Mentions")+
  scale_y_continuous(n.breaks = 15) +
    scale_x_date(
    breaks = artificial_intelligence$start_date,
    date_labels = "%b %Y"  
  ) +
  theme_minimal()+
   theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 25,  hjust=1),
     plot.margin = margin(10, 10, 35, 10)
  )
  
```
**Q5** 
What school has had the most classes removed as the semesters go by? (Or calculate the percent change from the department

**A5**
There was not one semester that had the same exact courses as another (which makes sense with the winter and summer classes.) While the Business department has the most courses provided with the data frame, it wasn't even on top 20 of the departments with the highest percent change. Departments like University Honors, Physics, and School of Music had an average percent change of courses provided over 1000 percent. While Global Communities, Executive MBA Program, Office of Undergraduate Research had negative average percent change of courses provided throughout semester. 

```{r}
department_ref <- umd_courses |>
  separate_rows(department, sep = ";") |>
  mutate(department = trimws(department)) |>
  select(department) |>
  distinct()

department_ref

#classes per semester 

classes_per_department <- umd_courses |>
  separate_rows(department, sep = ";") |>
  mutate(department = trimws(department)) |>
  group_by(department)|>
  summarize(class_count = n())
  
classes_per_department 


#-- SEMESTERS--# 

#terms ref 
termsem <- umd_courses |>
  select(term) |>
  distinct()|>
  arrange(desc(term))

termsem

#There's 22 terms in this dataset. Should i create a  dataframe that filter each term and group by department to summarize the class count... 22 times OR find a loop code -->  I'll try to create a loop 
   
#trying out loops, trying to remember if the python rules apply
   
#Making a vector with the list of terms I had outputted in previous data set
terms_vector <- unique(termsem$term)
 
#Make an empty list 
results_list_terms <- list()

#Creating loop using the for every term in the term list vector, they will output results...
 
for (term in terms_vector) {
  results <- umd_courses |>
    separate_rows(department, sep = ";") |>
  mutate(department = trimws(department))|>
  filter(term == !!term) |> # the !! forces the code to look at the values under term column as its own dataframe so that the filter can work -- only a tidyverse thing 
  group_by(department)|>
  summarize(class_count = n())
  
  results <- results |> mutate(term = term)
results_list_terms[[as.character(term)]] <-results
}

final_term_list <- bind_rows(results_list_terms,.id = "term")


#Widening the data set so it's easier to read. So that each term is in its own column instead of a part of a terms row. Essentially flipping the data frame  axis
depart_class_termlist  <- final_term_list|>
  pivot_wider(names_from = term, #specifying the unique term semesters are their own column name 
              values_from = class_count, #class_count values will transfer to new columns; under each term
              names_prefix = "term_") 

#Joining the total classes dataframe into the previous one 
depart_class_termlist_2 <- depart_class_termlist |>
  left_join(classes_per_department, by = "department") |>
    rename(
      total_count = class_count 
      #should i rename the term columns? lazy rn no shade. 
    )


#print tibble
depart_class_termlist 
  


avg_percent_change <- depart_class_termlist |>
  select(department, starts_with("term_")) |> 
  pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("term_"),  #long format
               names_to = "term", 
               values_to = "class_count") |> 
  group_by(department) |>  
  arrange(term) |>  #  the terms are in order i guess
  mutate(percent_change = (class_count - lag(class_count)) / lag(class_count) * 100) |>  # percent change
  summarise(average_percent_change = mean(percent_change, na.rm = TRUE)) |> 
  ungroup() 


#arrange from high percent change to low
avg_percent_change |>
  arrange(desc(average_percent_change))



```
